title: He failed. Not math.

creative.thesis: A fail is a total; the parts tell the story. Einstein failed an entrance exam on languages, never math.
creative.opening: the 1935 headline clipping slams onto a big wooden report-card board
creative.composition: a giant 1890s report-card board on a school wall: one row per subject, each grade a chunky wooden tile (a cube) that rolls to show its number; a 1-6 scale ruler that can flip
creative.rhythm: headline, his reply, the 1895 exam split into parts, the 1896 certificate tiles rolling to 6 6 6 3, a hard flip of the scale ruler, the rule card
creative.payoff: the total stamp FAIL breaks into its parts; the viewer is told to read the parts
creative.sound: wooden clacks for each tile, a stamp on FAIL, a ruler whoosh on the flip

_note: Rendered in raea (raea/ungraded-008-einstein): a report-card board of rolling grade tiles; cues live in the composition.

beats.say: "Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics." A real headline. Einstein read it, and laughed.
In {1935|nineteen thirty-five} he told a rabbi in Princeton: "I never failed in mathematics." Before fifteen, he had mastered calculus.
So where's the fail? {1895|Eighteen ninety-five}. He's sixteen, two years early, sitting the entrance exam of Zurich's Polytechnic.
Math and physics: top marks. Languages and the rest: not enough. Overall: fail.
The school's director tells him: finish high school first. So he spends a year at a small school in Aarau.
His final certificate, {1896|eighteen ninety-six}. Algebra: six. Geometry: six. Physics: six. French: three.
One theory for the myth: that year, the school flipped its scale. Read the old way, his sixes look like fails.
At school, a fail sounds like a verdict on you. Out here, it's a list.
So next time you fail a test, don't say: I'm bad at this. Read the parts. Find the one that failed.
A year later, Einstein got in. French: still a three. And that headline? Still going around.
